source_text: Reprobat etiam illos qui iubeant cibis abstinere, sed de prouidentia spiritus sancti, praedamnans iam haereticos perpetuam abstinentiam praecepturos ad destruenda et despicienda opera creatoris, quales inueniam apud Marcionem, apud Tatianum, apud Iouem, hodiernum de Pythagora haereticum, non . apud paracletum. quantula est enim apud nos interdictio ciborum? duas in anno hebdomadas xerophagiarum nec totas, exceptis scilicet sabbatis et dominicis, offerimus deo abstinentes ab eis quae non reicimus, sed differimus. atqui ad Romanos scribens uos nunc compungit detractatores\' huius officii. ne . propter pabulum solueritis, inquit, opus dei. quod opus? de quo ait: bonum est carnem non edere et uinum non potare. nam qui in istis seruit, placabilis et propitiabilis deo nostro est. quidam credit omnia manducanda esse, quidam autem infirmus holera uescitur; qui manducat, ne nullificet non manducantem. tu quis es, qui alienum seruum iudicas? et qui manducat et qui non manducat, deo agit gratias. cum autem humano arbitrio uetet controuersiam fieri, quanto magis diuino? ita sciebat quosdam castigatores et interdictores uictus incusare, qui ex fastidio, non qui ex officio abstinerent, probare uero qui in honorem, non qui in conuicium creatoris. et si claues macelli tibi tradidit permittens esui omnia ad constituendam idolothytorum exceptionem, non tamen in macello regnum dei inclusit. nec enim, inquit, esus aut potus est dei regnum, et, esca nos deo non commendat, non ut de arida dictum putes, sed potius de uncta et accurata, siquidem subiciens: nec si manducauerimus, abundabimus, nec si non manducauerimus, deficiemus, tibi magis intonat, qui abundare te existimas, si edas, et deficere, si non edas, et ideo ista detractas. dominum quoque quam indigne ad tuam libidinem interpretaris passim manducantem et bibentem, sed puto, quod etiam ieiunarit, qui beatos non saturatos, sed esurientes et sitientes pronuntiarit, qui escam profitebatur, non quam discipuli existimarant, sed paterni operis perfectionem, docens operari escam quae permanet in uitam aeternam, in ordinaria etiam oratione panem mandans postulandum, non et Attalicas diuitias. sic et Esaias non negauit deum elegisse ieiunium, sed quale non elegerit enumerauit. in diebus enim, inquit, ieiuniorum uestrorum inueniuntur uoluntates uestrae, et omnes subiectos uobis succutitis aut ad conuicia et lites ieiunatis et caeditis pugnis. non tale ieiunium ego elegi, sed quale subiecit, et subiciendo non abstulit, sed confirmauit.
thought_title: The apostle's own words condemn the critics of fasting
orientation: Tertullian is answering opponents who cite Paul against food restrictions, and he now turns Paul's words back on them.
pass_a_gloss: He also reproves those who would command people to abstain from foods, but from the providence of the Holy Spirit, already condemning in advance heretics who would prescribe perpetual abstinence for destroying and despising the works of the Creator, such as I would find among Marcion, among Tatian, among Jove, a modern heretic from Pythagoras, not among the Advocate. For how small is the prohibition of foods among us? Two weeks in the year of dry-food fasts, and not whole ones, excepting of course the Sabbaths and the Lord's days, we offer to God, abstaining from things which we do not reject, but postpone. But writing to the Romans he now pricks you, detractors of this duty. Lest, he says, for the sake of food you destroy the work of God. What work? The one about which he says: it is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine. For he who serves in these things is appeasing and propitiating to our God. One person believes all things must be eaten, but another, being weak, feeds on vegetables; let the one who eats not nullify the one who does not eat. You, who are you, who judge another's servant? Both the one who eats and the one who does not eat gives thanks to God. But when he forbids controversy to be made by human judgment, how much more by divine? Thus he knew that certain chastisers and forbidders of food were being accused who abstained from disdain, not from duty, but that those were approved who did so in honor, not in insult of the Creator. And if he handed over to you the keys of the meat market, permitting all things for eating for establishing the exception of idol-sacrificed things, he did not however enclose the kingdom of God in the meat market. For neither, he says, is eating or drinking the kingdom of God, and, food does not commend us to God, not so that you think it was said about dry food, but rather about rich and elaborate food, since indeed he adds: neither if we eat will we abound, nor if we do not eat will we lack, he thunders rather at you, who think that you abound if you eat, and lack if you do not eat, and therefore you disparage these things. The Lord too how unworthily you interpret according to your desire as eating and drinking everywhere, but I think that he also fasted, who pronounced blessed not the filled, but the hungry and thirsty, who professed food, not what the disciples had supposed, but the completion of the Father's work, teaching to work the food which remains into eternal life, in the ordinary prayer also commanding bread to be asked for, not Attalic riches. Thus also Isaiah did not deny that God chose fasting, but he enumerated what kind he did not choose. For in the days, he says, of your fasts your wills are found, and all those subjected to you you shake, or you fast for quarrels and lawsuits and strike with fists. Not such a fast did I choose, but such as he added, and by adding he did not take away, but confirmed.

pass_b_english: He also reproves those who would command people to abstain from foods—but on the basis of the Holy Spirit's providence, condemning in advance the heretics who would prescribe perpetual abstinence in order to destroy and despise the Creator's works. Such people I find among Marcion, among Tatian, among Ioues, that modern heretic derived from Pythagoras—but not among the Advocate. For how small is our restriction of foods? We offer to God two weeks of dry-food fasts in the year, and not even complete weeks, excluding of course the Sabbaths and Lord's days, abstaining from things we do not reject but merely postpone. And yet, writing to the Romans, he now stings you as detractors of this duty. "Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food," he says (Romans 14:20). What work? The one about which he says: "It is good not to eat meat or drink wine" (Romans 14:21). For the one who serves in these matters is pleasing and acceptable to our God. "One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables; let the one who eats not nullify the one who does not eat" (Romans 14:2-3). "Who are you to judge another man's servant?" (Romans 14:4). "Both the one who eats and the one who does not eat gives thanks to God" (Romans 14:6). But when he forbids controversy to arise by human judgment, how much more by divine judgment? So he knew that some accuse those who discipline and restrict their diet—people who abstain from disdain, not from duty—but approve those who do so in honor of the Creator, not in insult to him. And if he handed you the keys of the meat market, permitting everything to be eaten in order to establish the exception for idol-sacrificed things, he did not therefore shut up the kingdom of God in the meat market. For he says, "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking" (Romans 14:17), and "Food does not commend us to God" (1 Corinthians 8:8)—not so that you should think this was said about dry food, but rather about rich and elaborate food. Indeed, when he adds, "If we eat, we are no better off, and if we do not eat, we are no worse off" (1 Corinthians 8:8), he thunders more at you, who think you are better off if you eat and worse off if you do not, and that is why you disparage these practices. How unworthily you also interpret the Lord to suit your own appetite, as one who ate and drank indiscriminately. But I think that he also fasted—he who pronounced blessed not those who are full, but those who hunger and thirst (Matthew 5:6); he who declared his food to be not what the disciples supposed, but the completion of the Father's work (John 4:34), teaching them to work for the food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27); who in the ordinary prayer commanded us to ask for bread (Matthew 6:11), not for Attalic riches. So too Isaiah did not deny that God had chosen fasting, but he listed what kind of fasting God had not chosen. "In the days of your fasts," he says, "your own desires are found, and you oppress all who are subject to you; you fast for quarrels and strife and strike with the fist. I did not choose such a fast" (Isaiah 58:3-5)—but the kind he went on to describe, and by describing it he did not take away fasting but confirmed it.
